articles.title: Prehistoric human life revealed at Saudi lakeside site
articles.summary: A recently discovered lakeside site in southern Saudi Arabia has yielded a wealth of information about prehistoric human life in the region.
articles.content: A recently discovered lakeside site in southern Saudi Arabia has yielded a wealth of information about prehistoric human life in the region. The ancient lake, which dates back around 125,000 years, was once home to a thriving ecosystem and a diverse range of plant and animal species. Researchers from King Abdullah University of Science and Technology have been working alongside colleagues from Griffith University and other international institutions to unravel the secrets of the site, known as Uruq al-Julaybah. By combining insights from geology, archaeology, botany, and micropaleontology, the team has gained a detailed understanding of how early humans lived in this part of Arabia. A key factor in the region's history is its climate, which was once much wetter and greener than it is today. The researchers have found evidence of a relatively stable freshwater lake surrounded by vegetation and open grasslands, providing a unique window into the past. To reconstruct the ancient landscape, the team used satellite terrain modeling to create a detailed map of the 340-square-kilometer area surrounding the lake. This work was complemented by systematic grid surveys to collect fossils and stone tools from the site. The researchers also employed advanced dating methods, including two different techniques applied to sand and fossil teeth, to determine the age of the finds. Additionally, they used 3D-refitting techniques to analyze the structure of stone tools and microscopic and chemical residue analysis to examine tool surfaces for signs of wear. Further evidence of early human presence was uncovered through the discovery of rare plant material and megafauna remains at the site. The fossil record at the site is remarkably diverse, with over 500 specimens of plants and animals documented across more than 130 locations. This bounty includes a range of invertebrates, as well as larger animal remains such as hippos, long-horned buffaloes, camels, Arabian oryx, gazelles, and ostriches. Researchers have collected an impressive number of stone tools from the main study area, with over 5,511 specimens larger than 2 cm in size. The majority of these tools were crafted from flint, a material that was extensively used for this purpose. Analysis has revealed that many of these tools employ Levallois techniques, a method of stone tool production that is both complex and sophisticated. The presence of plant residues on the stone tools provides valuable insights into the daily lives of the people who occupied the site. These residues include not only edible plants but also those with toxic properties, suggesting that the inhabitants were capable of processing and utilizing a wide range of plant materials for various purposes. Some of the most significant findings from the site relate to the potential use of toxic plant compounds in hunting technology. This is an intriguing discovery, as it suggests that early humans in this region may have employed innovative methods to enhance their hunting prowess. Additionally, evidence of palm-related vegetation has been uncovered, which adds to our understanding of the local flora and fauna. The uniqueness of this site lies in its ability to provide a comprehensive picture of daily life for the people who inhabited Green Arabia. The presence of animal remains, stone tools, and plant material, all found together in a single context, offers a rare glimpse into the lives of early humans. This combination of elements has allowed researchers to reconstruct with remarkable detail how these individuals lived, hunted, and interacted with their environment. The shores of ancient Lake Mundafan were a hub of activity 125,000 years ago, attracting a diverse array of freshwater resources, animals, plants, and raw materials. This convergence of elements enabled early humans to engage in various activities such as crafting stone tools, preparing hunting equipment, processing animal and plant resources, and working with fibers. The presence of these resources suggests that the lake's shores were an ideal location for human settlement during this period. Professor Frans van Buchem expresses his enthusiasm for the collaborative effort that has made this reconstruction possible, highlighting the unique value of bringing together specialists from diverse fields to create a comprehensive picture of life in the distant past. The expertise of these researchers has allowed them to shed light on aspects of ancient human behavior and environmental interactions. Dr. Faisal Al-Jibreen describes the discovery as an important archaeological find that provides valuable insights into the early prehistory of southern Saudi Arabia, particularly with regard to the relationship between humans, animals, and their environment during this period. The significance of this site lies in its ability to offer a detailed and nuanced view of how people lived in a landscape vastly different from modern-day Arabia. The combination of animal remains, stone tools, and plant material within a single, dated context makes this discovery truly remarkable. The discovery is significant because it provides a unique window into the lives of early humans living in Saudi Arabia 125,000 years ago. The site's location near a lake suggests that these individuals were able to thrive in a relatively stable and wet environment. This finding highlights the importance of building heritage science capabilities in Saudi Arabia, allowing researchers to uncover even the smallest traces of human activity from the past. Professor Laurence Hapiot notes that this capability will enable them to turn such discoveries into compelling stories. articles.title: Apple CarPlay Warns Drivers of Speed Cameras
articles.summary: A new feature in Apple CarPlay allows users to receive warnings about speed cameras while driving through their chosen navigation apps.
articles.content: A new feature in Apple CarPlay allows users to receive warnings about speed cameras while driving, but these alerts come from their chosen navigation apps, not directly from CarPlay itself. Navigation apps such as Waze and Google Maps can provide real-time information on the location of speed cameras, giving drivers a heads up before they reach them. However, it's essential to note that mobile speed traps are often in motion and may not be accounted for by these apps unless someone reports their new position through the app. The concept of mobile speed detectors dates back to 1899 when a NYC taxicab driver named Jacob German was caught speeding at 12mph in an 8mph zone. At the time, police officers on bicycles were used as mobile units to patrol roads and enforce speed limits. While modern technology has improved significantly since then, there is no single navigation app that can provide real-time information on every camera location. This is because speed cameras often move around or are not reported in a timely manner by drivers. Despite these limitations, navigation apps continue to play an essential role in helping drivers avoid speeding fines and stay safe on the road. When using Apple Maps on CarPlay, users don't have a switch to toggle on or off camera alerts in supported regions. Instead, these alerts are automatically activated when navigating through areas where speed cameras are present. This means drivers can stay informed without having to manually adjust settings. Waze, one of the compatible navigation apps for CarPlay, offers more control over camera alerts. By default, Waze turns on camera warnings, but users can fine-tune them in the app's Settings menu. To make these changes, navigate to Alerts and Reports > Reports > Cameras and toggle on or off specific types of cameras. For those who want to customize their settings further, Google Maps on CarPlay offers similar options. Users can tap "Report" to report mobile speed camera locations, which will be visible to other drivers using the app. To receive alerts from other drivers, open Settings > Alert options and select All alerts. Some third-party navigation apps also provide warning alerts for speed cameras, even when not actively navigating. Radarbot is one such app that sends alerts for fixed and red light cameras through CarPlay, but only with a Gold membership. Other apps like Roadar offer additional features, including Flock camera detection and license plate reader notifications. Radarbot isn't the only option for drivers concerned about speed cameras. For those specifically interested in Flock cameras, there's also FlockHopper, a free app that works with CarPlay to provide alerts and warnings when navigating through areas where these cameras are present. To access warnings about speed cameras in Apple CarPlay, you'll need to navigate through your chosen navigation app's settings. For those using Apple Maps, the Speed Limit toggle can be found in Settings > Apps > Maps > Driving. Once enabled, the posted limit will appear on screen while navigating. This feature is a useful addition for drivers who want to stay informed about speed limits without having to constantly check signs or road markings. If you're using Waze instead of Apple Maps, make sure you disconnect from CarPlay and open the Waze app to access its settings. Within Settings > Speedometer > Show Speedometer > Set Preferences > Show Speed Limit, you can enable the display of speed limits. This feature is also available in Google Maps, where it's located in a similar section of the app. Google Maps and Waze both offer additional features that provide warnings when drivers exceed speed limits or approach areas with sharply changing limits. These apps are integrated into CarPlay, but not all users may be aware of these capabilities, particularly those who have upgraded to CarPlay Ultra. articles.content: A popular feature in newer cars makes it easy to navigate and access various iPhone features while driving, but some manufacturers have chosen not to support this technology. To determine if a car supports Apple CarPlay, one can start by checking online for a comprehensive list maintained by the company itself. The list covers nearly all new models from major brands, making it a valuable resource for potential buyers looking to make an informed decision when purchasing a vehicle. However, there are some notable exceptions to this rule, with Tesla and Rivian being two prominent manufacturers that have opted out of supporting CarPlay in their vehicles. Additionally, General Motors had previously considered abandoning support for Apple's software on newer models in favor of its own alternative, but has since reversed this decision and reinstated CarPlay compatibility. For those looking to check if a specific car model supports wireless CarPlay integration, there are several options available. This can be done by accessing the iPhone settings and searching for the car's name among the list of available devices when Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are enabled on both the phone and the vehicle. To verify wireless connectivity in person, one can follow these steps: enable Bluetooth and Wi-Fi on the iPhone, then set the car's dashboard to Bluetooth or wireless mode. Next, press the voice command button on the steering wheel, after which the car should appear as an available device in Settings > General > CarPlay on the iPhone, confirming whether it supports wireless integration. Connecting a phone to a car's USB port will trigger a prompt to activate wired CarPlay if the vehicle supports it. This is a straightforward way to determine whether a car has integrated CarPlay support. However, not all cars with integrated CarPlay display this option on their dashboard screens or on the USB ports. Some cars may have a CarPlay symbol on the USB port, but even supported vehicles may not always feature this emblem. If you don't see either of these indicators, it's likely that your car doesn't have built-in CarPlay support. For drivers with cars lacking integrated CarPlay, there are alternative ways to add the technology, albeit at some expense and hassle. One option is to purchase a third-party screen designed for CarPlay integration. These screens can be mounted on the dashboard, effectively replacing or supplementing the existing display. These aftermarket screens, available from various manufacturers, can connect with both CarPlay and Android Auto systems. As a result, they enable users to access all software functions in any vehicle. Typically priced around $100 or less, these third-party screens are also portable, allowing for easy transfer between cars. Replacing your car's stereo receiver and screen with a new one that supports Apple CarPlay can be a more permanent solution, but it requires some technical expertise or a professional installation. This option involves purchasing a head unit specifically designed for CarPlay compatibility, which may still fit within a budget of $100 or less. While the cost of this approach might be comparable to buying just a screen, the installation process is often more complex and may necessitate paying someone to do it correctly. However, having an integrated CarPlay-compatible unit can simplify the overall setup and eliminate the need for additional peripherals. articles.title: Optical Illusions Have Been Used in Art and Architecture for Thousands of Years
articles.summary: Optical illusions have long been a source of fascination for many people around the world.
articles.content: Optical illusions have long been a source of fascination for many people around the world. These mind-bending images can trick our eyes and brains into seeing something that isn't really there, making them both perplexing and exciting at the same time. They often involve multiple subjects or scenes, but initially appear as only one image. It's not until we take a closer look and "bend our brains that we might start to see two different images emerge. When first presented with an optical illusion, it can be difficult to make out what is being shown. We may struggle to distinguish between multiple subjects or scenes, or even question whether the image is meant to depict something entirely different. However, as our brains begin to process the information, we might start to see things in a new light, literally. The thrill of discovery comes when we finally figure out what's going on and can see two separate images for what they are. This moment of realization can be both exhilarating and humbling, leaving us wondering how our brains were able to deceive us for so long. The history of optical illusions is a long and winding road that stretches back thousands of years. Cave art from around 30,000 BCE in New Delhi's Museum of Illusions provides some of the earliest evidence of these mind-bending creations. Drawings with crossed lines and strokes were used to represent movement, making it harder for our brains to process what we're seeing. These early optical illusions were likely created by artists who wanted to add an extra layer of depth and meaning to their work. As civilizations evolved, so did the use of optical illusions in art and architecture. In ancient Greece, around 500 BCE, philosophers and intellectuals experimented with these mind-bending techniques. They incorporated intricate mosaic designs into buildings and used curved columns that seemed straight at first glance. These early attempts at creating optical illusions were not just aesthetically pleasing but also served a purpose. By challenging our perceptions and forcing us to question what we see, they sparked conversations about the nature of reality itself. The ancient Greeks were not just philosophers and intellectuals, but also masters of optical illusions in architecture. In 500 BCE, they incorporated intricate mosaic designs into their buildings, which still mesmerize viewers today. The Parthenon's columns, for instance, appear to be curved at first glance, but upon closer inspection, they seem straight. The Renaissance period saw a significant shift in the use of optical illusions, with artists employing perspective and anamorphic art to create mind-bending effects. Leonardo da Vinci was a pioneer in this field, using depth techniques to make his compositions seem three-dimensional on flat surfaces. His works, such as The Last Supper, showcase this skill. Da Vinci's use of depth techniques in The Last Supper is particularly noteworthy, as it would manipulate the viewer's eye to go in his compositions," according to the artist himself. This manipulation of perception creates a sense of depth and dimensionality that draws the viewer in. Artists of the past century experimented with perspective and anamorphic art to create a sense of depth and dimensionality on flat surfaces. By using reflective surfaces, artists like Hans Holbein were able to hide objects in their works that could only be seen from specific angles. As the 19th century unfolded, psychologists began to explore the realm of optical illusions as a means to understand how our brains process conflicting visual signals. They created experiments that demonstrated differences in size, contrast, and brightness to uncover how our minds interpret what we see. These experiments relied on the idea that observing an illusion could reveal something about the workings of the brain. Psychologists believed that by creating illusions, they could gain insight into the way our brains process and interpret visual information. In 1995, Professor Edward H. Adelson created a notable example of this concept. The concept of optical illusions has been harnessed by various artists and performers to create captivating experiences for their audiences. Photographers have employed optical illusions in their work to make images more engaging and thought-provoking, while magicians use them to add an element of surprise and wonder to their tricks. This creative application of optical illusions has become a staple of modern entertainment. Museums dedicated entirely to optical illusions offer immersive experiences that challenge visitors' perceptions and understanding of reality. The use of tunnels, mirrors, and interactive artwork creates an environment where the mind is pushed to its limits. articles.title: Goodbye, overtourism? Sustainable travel gains ground
articles.summary: As tourism booms across Latin America, alternative forms of travel are gaining ground. Making your holiday more sustainable means rethinking who calls the shots, who invests and who benefits.

articles.title: South America Sees 7% Rise in International Tourism Last Year
articles.summary: International tourism figures reveal that South America saw a 7% surge in arrivals last year, while Central America experienced a 5% increase.
articles.content: International tourism figures reveal a 7% surge in arrivals to South America last year, exceeding the global average, while Central America saw a 5% increase. These statistics, released by UN Tourism, highlight the region's growing appeal as a travel destination. However, this boom comes with significant environmental and social costs. The sheer volume of visitors is straining local resources, causing tensions among residents and sparking questions about who benefits from tourism. As destinations become increasingly crowded, concerns over sustainability are escalating. Machu Picchu, Peru's iconic Inca citadel, has become a prime example of the problems caused by overtourism. With up to 5,600 visitors daily, local authorities have warned that the site is at risk of being added to UNESCO's List of World Heritage in Danger. This warning was issued in 2025 and followed expressions of concern from the UNESCO World Heritage Committee. Peru is not alone in its efforts to mitigate the impact of tourism on fragile ecosystems. Ecuador has taken steps to protect the Galapagos Islands by doubling entrance fees for foreign visitors to $200 in 2024. Despite this measure, pressure remains to develop new infrastructure, including hotels and tourist apartments. The influx of tourists into Mexico City's neighborhoods, such as Roma and Condesa, has also led to protests over rising rents. Digital nomads and travelers have contributed to increased demand for housing, exacerbating tensions between residents and business owners. The shift towards sustainable travel is gaining momentum as tour operators and travelers alike acknowledge the need for change. Regional managers like Richard Bazan are at the forefront of this movement, promoting community-based tourism that benefits local communities directly. Group sizes are decreasing, with travelers now opting for more intimate experiences rather than large-scale tours. This trend is driven by a desire to connect with destinations on a deeper level and foster meaningful interactions with locals. According to Bazan, tour groups have shrunk from 20 people to just four or five individuals. The concept of "nature-positive" tourism is also taking hold, with travel programs that support conservation efforts such as reforestation projects. Even traditional all-inclusive resorts are recognizing the need to break down their barriers and offer authentic experiences that allow visitors to engage with local communities. Community-based tourism has evolved from a niche market to a mainstream trend, with more travelers seeking out immersive experiences that benefit the places they visit. Bazan notes that this shift in consumer behavior is driving change within the industry as tour operators adapt to meet growing demand for sustainable travel options. The pressure for sustainability is also coming from travelers themselves, who are increasingly aware of tourism's impact on local communities and the environment. According to a recent survey by Booking.com, 93% of respondents expressed a desire to make more sustainable travel choices, with over half acknowledging the importance of considering local community needs when traveling. Financial barriers often hinder community-led sustainable tourism initiatives, as they lack access to affordable and flexible funding options. Tourism is typically viewed as a high-risk sector by financial institutions, leading them to offer expensive and inflexible products that can be detrimental to local communities' interests. In contrast, the foundation's fund offers low-interest loans with flexible repayment terms, allowing communities to manage their own projects without being burdened by excessive debt. Community-based tourism requires more than just a willingness to participate; it demands genuine partnership and collaboration between tourists, local residents, and external stakeholders. Effective ecotourism initiatives must be designed in close consultation with the community, ensuring that they are not imposed from outside but rather developed as a collective effort. Measuring the impact of community-based tourism can be challenging due to its social effects that extend beyond numerical data. A notable example is the Indigenous Mixtec community in Mexico, where tourists interested in learning the local language have sparked an interest among children who previously only spoke Spanish. These visitors are now attending language classes and even asking their grandparents to teach them Mixtec, a trend that highlights the long-term value of community-based tourism. By prioritizing cultural and regional diversity, this approach can create lasting benefits for both locals and travelers alike. While change in tourism practices is gradual, experts believe it's a worthwhile effort as it fosters greater respect for local communities and their environments, ultimately leading to happier outcomes for all parties involved. articles.title: Voyager 1 Sets Record for Distant Communication
articles.summary: The Voyager 1 spacecraft will soon mark a significant milestone in its half-century history as it becomes so distant from Earth that signals take a full day to be received.
articles.content: NASA's Voyager 1 probe has been the farthest human-made object in space for decades, but it's about to set another record that celebrates its enduring legacy. On November 18, the spacecraft will be so distant from Earth that it takes a full 24 hours for light to make the journey back. This means that any signal sent from Earth to Voyager 1 at this point would have to wait an entire day to be received. The achievement marks a significant milestone in the mission's half-century history, which began with the launch of the twin Voyager probes in September 1977. Despite being designed to operate for just five years, the spacecraft have far outlived many of the engineers who built them and continue to provide valuable data on the outer solar system. The Voyager probes have made some of the closest observations of the distant planets in our solar system, including flybys of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Researchers who worked on the Voyager program are now reflecting on its accomplishments and what's next for the spacecraft as they move into interstellar space. Pascal Lee, a planetary scientist at the SETI Institute who was part of the Voyager 2 team during its Neptune flyby in 1989, notes that the Voyagers have transcended generations. They continue to provide insights into our solar system and beyond, long after many of their creators have passed on. The Voyager probes are now about 16 billion miles from Earth, a distance that's equivalent to one light-day. This means it takes 24 hours for any signal sent from Earth to reach the spacecraft, making communication a slow but not impossible process. As Voyager 1 continues on its journey into interstellar space, scientists are reminded of the vastness of space and time. "It's still pathetically slow in the grand scheme of things," a team member noted, commenting on the pace at which communication is possible with the spacecraft. The sheer scale of the solar system becomes apparent when considering Voyager 1's current location. Although it has traveled beyond the heliosphere, the bubble of plasma blown outward by the sun that shields the planets from cosmic radiation, it still remains within the sun's gravitational grasp. This gravitational influence extends far beyond the Oort Cloud, a vast spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the solar system. Voyager 1 will need approximately 300 years to reach the cloud's inner edge and potentially up to 30,000 years to exit its vicinity altogether, according to NASA estimates. Despite its slow progress, Voyager 1 is steadily moving further away from Earth. It will eventually pass within a mere 7 light-years of the dim star Gliese 445 in about 40,000 years, at which point it will be closer to that star than our own sun. As for its trajectory, Voyager 1's path diverges significantly from that of its twin, Voyager 2. Launched in 1977, Voyager 2 took a different route through the solar system, swinging past Uranus and Neptune after revisiting Jupiter and Saturn. Currently situated about 13 billion miles from Earth, Voyager 2 will reach its own light-day mark in November 2035, according to NASA predictions. As Voyager 1 continues its journey into interstellar space, scientists are reflecting on what it means for communication with the spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. At this point, the time it takes for radio signals to travel between Earth and Voyager 1 becomes significant, with a signal taking 24 hours to reach the probe and another 24 hours for a response to make its way back. This means that if you want to send a message to Voyager 1, you can expect to wait two days before receiving a reply, according to Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. The increasing distance between Earth and Voyager 1 is not the only challenge facing the probe; it's also being affected by its own age. As the probe relies on nuclear batteries to generate power, the supply of energy is gradually dwindling due to the natural decay of plutonium, which is used to convert heat into electricity. This limited energy source forces NASA to carefully manage the use of nonessential instruments in order to conserve what remains and extend the mission for as long as possible. As Voyager 1 ventures further into interstellar space, scientists are reflecting on its groundbreaking discoveries that have transformed our understanding of the outer solar system. The spacecraft has been instrumental in uncovering hidden secrets about Jupiter's moon Europa, which was once a blurry speck but is now recognized as a remarkably smooth and geologically young world. One of the most significant findings made by Voyager 1 was the discovery of active volcanoes on Jupiter's moon Io, which was first spotted in 1979. This revelation provided scientists with a new perspective on the moon's surface, sparking further research into its geological processes. The presence of these volcanoes also highlighted the potential for life beyond Earth. The Voyager missions have laid the groundwork for numerous follow-up explorations, including NASA's Galileo mission to Jupiter and the Cassini mission to Saturn. These studies have significantly advanced our understanding of the solar system's dynamics and complexities. By probing the outer reaches of our cosmic neighborhood, scientists are gaining insights into the intricate relationships between planets, moons, and their environments. The Voyager spacecraft have been instrumental in challenging traditional notions about interstellar space as an empty vacuum. Instead, data collected from these probes suggests that it is a dynamic and complex frontier, teeming with magnetic fields, plasma, and cosmic rays. This understanding has profound implications for our comprehension of the universe's evolution and the potential for life beyond Earth. As Voyager 1 continues its journey, scientists are grappling with the issue of power conservation. The spacecraft was designed to operate with limited energy reserves, forcing NASA to carefully manage the use of nonessential instruments to extend the mission's lifespan. This delicate balancing act is crucial in ensuring that the probe remains operational for as long as possible. The Voyager missions have also provided us with a unique perspective on the solar system's structure and composition. By collecting data from the outer planets, scientists are gaining a deeper understanding of their atmospheric profiles, including those of Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. This knowledge has far-reaching implications for our comprehension of planetary formation and evolution. The discoveries made by Voyager 1 have not only expanded our understanding of the solar system but also paved the way for future explorations. As scientists continue to analyze data from these missions, they are refining their theories about the universe's origins and the potential for life beyond Earth. The Voyager spacecraft's power-saving reconfigurations have been crucial in keeping it operational for nearly 50 years. Engineers have implemented various measures to extend its lifespan, including shutting off high-power subsystems and switching on lower-power alternatives. One such effort, dubbed the "Big Bang, has bought the team almost two more years without having to turn off any instrument, according to Perry. As the onboard power dwindles, there's a growing recognition that it won't be operational forever, notes Deana Weibel, an anthropologist at Grand Valley State University in Michigan. The science mission will be considered complete when no science instruments are operational, and the team has decided to keep the magnetometer as the last remaining instrument. Even after the science data stops coming in, both Voyager probes may continue sending back basic engineering updates until around 2036, according to NASA's projections. Despite their eventual silence, the spacecraft will remain intact, allowing scientists to calculate their positions based on their speed and trajectories even after they fall silent. The Golden Records carried by Voyager 1 are more than just a scientific tool - they're also an artistic expression of human culture and identity. These records contain a diverse array of sounds, including natural phenomena like wind and animal calls, as well as greetings in 55 languages to potentially introduce humanity to any extraterrestrial civilization that might encounter them. The records also include images of Earth and a celestial map pinpointing the location of our planet. This collection of human creations is intended for a hypothetical civilization capable of retrieving and interpreting these messages. The inclusion of visual instructions on how to play the records demonstrates the creative thinking behind this project, blurring the lines between science and art. The Golden Records can be seen as an artistic exercise in self-expression, reflecting humanity's capacity to convey its essence through various mediums. In contrast to the possibility of an alien civilization playing the record, scientists acknowledge that it is more likely for humans to recover Voyager 1 than for extraterrestrial life to find and interpret the messages. The chances of us going after Voyager 1 and bringing it back for the Smithsonian are more believable than any chance of an alien civilization finding it, one scientist noted. As the spacecraft continues its journey into interstellar space, the Golden Records remain a lasting symbol of humanity's presence on Earth, transcending individual lifetimes. Knowing that Voyager will continue its mission long past my lifetime actually gives me comfort," said Kelly Perry, a member of the Voyager team, highlighting the significance of this cosmic time capsule as a shared legacy of human endeavor. articles.title: Nvidia's Business Practices Under Fire by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has criticized Nvidia's exports to China, suggesting top executives would face consequences if it were a bank.
articles.content: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has unleashed a scathing critique of Nvidia's business practices, suggesting that if the company were a bank, several top executives would be fired. Bessent made these comments in an interview on Fox News' Sunday Morning Futures, where he was asked to explain why Megaspeed, a cloud computing firm linked to Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, did not get blacklisted. The Treasury Department had been pushing for trade restrictions against the company. The issue at hand revolves around Nvidia's exports of high-end chips to China, with the Trump administration having blocked certain models while allowing others. This move aims to preserve the US lead in the AI race. According to reports from The Information, Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary shipped a staggering $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips to China over two years. Bessent pointed out that this raises questions about Nvidia's compliance with US export restrictions. When asked about the Commerce Department's role in not blacklisting Megaspeed, Bessent shifted focus to Nvidia itself, saying that what matters most is whether the company has a culture of compliance around these restrictions. He wants to know if failures originated at lower levels or went all the way up to the C-suite. Bessent also expressed interest in knowing how Nvidia used shell companies and whether they served as workarounds to sell chips to China despite export restrictions. Nvidia's shakeup continues as the company navigates its leadership crisis. In a move that has left many in the tech industry talking, Colette Kress has been appointed interim CEO while the search for Huang's permanent replacement is underway. Rumors are swirling about who could take over the top spot at Nvidia on a permanent basis. Insiders believe Kress and Ian Buck, a key engineer at the company, have what it takes to lead Nvidia into its next chapter. However, outsiders such as Lisa Su from AMD and Rene Haas from Arm are also being considered for the role. Meanwhile, sources close to Huang suggest that he may be eyeing a return to the helm of the company. A "war room of Silicon Valley executives is reportedly mobilizing in an effort to persuade Nvidia's board to bring him back. Notably, some influential figures, including Elon Musk, are publicly voicing their support for Huang's reinstatement. Huang's potential return has sparked debate about whether it would be the right move for Nvidia. Some argue that the company needs a fresh start and that bringing back its former CEO could hinder progress. articles.title: Tsunami experts study lab experiments and real-world scenarios to understand volcanic eruptions' impact on sea waves
articles.summary: Researchers have conducted laboratory experiments to better grasp how volcanic rocks and ash interact with seawater to generate massive waves.
articles.content: Tsunami experts have long struggled to predict when a volcanic eruption will trigger a devastating tsunami, but new research is shedding light on this complex and poorly understood phenomenon. The main challenge lies in understanding how volcanic rocks and ash interact with seawater to generate massive waves. In an effort to better grasp the dynamics at play, researchers have turned to laboratory experiments, which provide valuable insights into the processes involved. However, it remains unclear whether these models accurately replicate real-world scenarios, making predictions a daunting task. To address this uncertainty, scientists have sought to compare lab results with actual observations from volcanic eruptions. The Italian island of Stromboli has emerged as an ideal location for studying tsunamis triggered by volcanic activity. The volcano's constant eruptions and frequent entry into the sea create an environment conducive to monitoring these events. A unique monitoring system, comprising land-based cameras and offshore wave gauges, provides valuable data on the formation and impact of tsunamis. The researchers' decision to focus on Stromboli was driven by its distinctive characteristics, which make it an ideal "laboratory in the field." By comparing lab results with real-world observations from this volcano, scientists aim to gain a deeper understanding of the complex interactions between volcanic materials and seawater. This knowledge could ultimately improve predictions and save lives in the event of a tsunami triggered by a volcanic eruption. The researchers conducted laboratory experiments to better understand how volcanic eruptions trigger tsunamis. They focused on three recent eruptions at Stromboli volcano that generated tsunamis between 2019 and 2021. The team compared observations from the field with results from both new and existing lab experiments. In the laboratory, a large tank filled with water was used to replicate the conditions of a volcanic eruption. A mass of polystyrene beads, representing pyroclastic flows, was released down a slope into the water. Despite being buoyant, these lightweight beads can still generate significant waves when sent tumbling into the water. The experiments revealed that lab simulations cannot be directly scaled up to predict real-world events, with most models based on such experiments overestimating tsunami sizes in the field. However, the new research helped bridge this gap by reproducing key features observed at Stromboli, including a distinctive three-wave pattern. The team's findings suggest that lab experiments can capture the energy transfer from pyroclastic flows to resulting wave trains, although some limitations remain. This knowledge could ultimately improve predictions and save lives in the event of a tsunami triggered by a volcanic eruption. The researchers' findings offer a crucial step forward in assessing volcanic tsunami hazards. By comparing lab experiments to real-world observations, the team was able to gain valuable insights into the dynamics of such events. This knowledge will be instrumental in refining predictions and mitigating the impact of tsunamis triggered by volcanic eruptions. The study's results have significant implications for disaster preparedness and response efforts. The research has provided a critical foundation for improving our understanding of the complex processes involved in volcanic tsunami generation. articles.title: Couch potato origins tied to TV's cathode-ray tube history
articles.summary: The term "couch potato" describes individuals who spend excessive time lounging on their couch and tend to be lazy or inactive.
articles.content: The term "couch potato has become a widely recognized way to describe someone who spends an excessive amount of time lounging on their couch, often glued to the TV. However, this colloquialism also has a broader meaning, encompassing individuals who tend to be lazy or inactive in general. They might not contribute as much as they could or should, and are often overly fond of their home comforts. The term potato in this context is likely due to the vegetable's ability to remain relatively unchanged and unassuming, much like a person who spends most of their time sitting still. This nickname suggests that someone referred to as a couch potato has become a bit stagnant, lacking the motivation or energy to engage in more active pursuits. The term couch potato is rooted in another colloquialism from the 20th century that has a fascinating etymology of its own. Television sets have been affectionately known as tubes since the 1950s, with this nickname referencing the cathode-ray tube that was the primary component inside many early TVs. The cathode-ray tube is essentially a vacuum picture tube consisting of a funnel-shaped glass container coated in phosphors, which emit light when struck by electrons. Inside the TV, the television signal enters through the back and triggers a stream of electrons from the cathode, firing them at the screen's interior where they cause the phosphors to glow and produce an image on the glass surface. The use of tube as a colloquialism for TVs likely arose because of the visible tubes inside early models that contained the cathode-ray technology. These early TV sets were often bulky and had exposed components, making their inner workings visible and contributing to the widespread adoption of the term tube in everyday language. The term tube has persisted in everyday language despite the fact that modern TVs have moved away from their clunky predecessors. These early tube televisions were often cumbersome and heavy due to their glass components. The widespread adoption of this technology led to its nickname becoming an integral part of popular culture. In the late 1950s, a new nickname emerged for television - the boob tube. This term carried a slightly different connotation than the original tube, implying that watching TV wasn't necessarily the best use of one's time. The notion of being a boob tuber eventually led to the coining of a more affectionate term: couch potato. In the late 1950s, a TV set began to be referred to as the boob tube, a name derived from the notion that watching television might make someone foolish. The term boob tuber was then used to describe individuals who spent excessive amounts of time watching TV. This label likely arose from the assumption that frequent viewers would become similarly dull-witted. As linguists often note, language is constantly evolving through a series of subtle changes and extensions. The term couch potato emerged in 1976 as an extension of the concept of a boob tuber." The inclusion of "couch in this new term suggests that someone who spends their time watching TV typically sits on their sofa at home, further emphasizing their sedentary lifestyle. The couch potato term gained widespread acceptance soon after its introduction in 1976, becoming a ubiquitous descriptor for individuals who spend excessive time watching TV. This colloquialism has managed to endure despite the decline of other related terms. In contrast, phrases like boob tube" and "boob tuber" seem to have largely fallen out of favor. articles.title: Facebook Accounts Remain Active After Owner's Death Unless Notified
articles.summary: Meta can take action on deceased user accounts once notified, allowing for memorialization or deletion.
articles.content: Facebook and Instagram accounts continue operating as usual after their owner's passing unless someone notifies Meta of the death. Meta can take action once aware of a user's demise, allowing for either deletion or "memorialization of the account based on the deceased's preferences and requests from relatives. When an account is memorialized, Meta adds a tag to indicate it's a remembering profile while keeping posts, photos, and videos intact for those who had access previously. Facebook also removes these profiles from friend suggestions and birthday reminders. However, relatives seeking to save memories or manage their loved one's account face significant hurdles, including limited access to private messages. Relatives wanting to plan ahead can do so by informing Meta of the deceased's wishes, but this doesn't grant them greater control over the account itself. Managing a deceased person's social media presence is becoming increasingly important as online interactions become more integral to our lives. To prepare for this scenario, Facebook allows users to designate a legacy contact who can manage their main profile after it has been memorialized. This designated individual can perform various tasks, including pinning posts about memorial services and editing the profile and cover photos. However, it's essential to note that the role of a legacy contact is limited in scope. They cannot log into the account, access private messages, or remove friends. Instead, they serve as a caretaker who can respond to incoming friend requests and request the removal of the account. This restricted power highlights the importance of clearly communicating one's wishes regarding their online presence. The process for designating a legacy contact is straightforward and takes place in the Accounts Center under Profiles and personal details > Account ownership and control > Memorialization . Here, users can either choose to appoint a contact or opt for the Delete after death" option. The latter requires proof of death before Meta removes the account entirely. When selecting the deletion option, it's worth noting that this choice applies not only to the main Facebook profile but also to any additional profiles associated with it. This comprehensive approach ensures that the deceased person's online presence is handled in a unified manner. When someone passes away without designating a contact to handle their online presence, friends and family can still request memorialization by providing documentation as proof. This process allows loved ones to preserve the deceased person's social media profiles in a respectful manner, even if there is no designated legacy contact. However, once a profile has been memorialized, it cannot be edited or updated without a legacy contact, who has been granted permission by the deceased to manage their online presence after they pass away. This limitation applies not only to Facebook but also to Instagram, which offers similar features and settings for handling a user's account after death. To request memorialization of an Instagram account, users must first report the death and provide supporting evidence, such as an obituary, before the process can be initiated. When an Instagram account is memorialized, it retains its original content and keeps its existing privacy settings intact, meaning that private accounts remain private even after the owner's passing. This approach allows families to maintain a sense of continuity without exposing personal information. The process for requesting memorialization doesn't provide any clear timeline for completion, leaving users uncertain about how long it will take to finalize their request.
